title: Compact One-Manifolds Have Two Shapes
notes: Open the appendix as a classification theorem rather than a bag of special cases. The local hypothesis says every point sees a line or half-line, while compactness forces only finitely many pieces after cutting, so the global answer collapses to interval or circle.

title: The Proof Route
notes: Use this route slide to give students a mental map before details arrive. The proof begins analytically with smooth coordinates and Morse cuts, then deliberately forgets most geometry and records only which interval components attach to which special points.

title: Local Models Are Severe
notes: Emphasize that one-dimensional manifold means a very small menu of neighborhoods. Interior points have two local directions, boundary points have one local direction, and that single observation will later prohibit a three-armed graph from being a manifold.

title: Smooth Repair Keeps Direction
notes: The smoothing lemma should be presented as a quality-control step. If a coordinate is assembled from monotone pieces, smoothing is allowed only when the repaired derivative stays positive, because positive derivative is what keeps the coordinate locally invertible.

title: Morse Cuts Make Finitely Many Pieces
notes: Connect compactness to finiteness here. A good height function has only finitely many critical points on a compact one-manifold, and boundary points are also recorded, so removing the special set produces finitely many open interval components.

title: Each Remaining Piece Is An Open Interval
notes: After the cuts, the hard smooth object becomes a list of standard interval pieces. The closure of one piece can meet the special set in one or two endpoint points, and this endpoint bookkeeping is exactly what becomes the incidence graph.

title: Coordinates On Components Are Monotone
notes: Make the inverse function theorem visible through this monotone coordinate picture. On a component away from critical points the derivative of the chosen coordinate does not vanish, so the component can be parameterized as a standard open interval.

title: Turn Closures Into An Incidence Graph
notes: The graph is not extra structure pulled from nowhere; it is the memory of how interval closures touch the finite cut set. Vertices are special points, edges are interval components, and each endpoint relation is a closure relation in the manifold.

title: No Vertex May Branch
notes: This is the decisive local-to-global constraint. If three interval components met at one special point, every small neighborhood would have three punctured arms, which cannot be homeomorphic to a line neighborhood or a half-line boundary neighborhood.

title: Degree At Most Two Forces Path Or Cycle
notes: Once the incidence graph is finite, connected, and has maximum degree at most two, there are no hidden graph types left. A connected graph with degree-one vertices is a path, while all vertices degree two gives a cycle.

title: Endpoint Count Detects Boundary
notes: Relate the graph endpoints back to manifold boundary. A path has exactly two degree-one ends and models a compact interval with two boundary points, while a cycle has no degree-one vertex and models a boundaryless circle component.

title: Gluing A Path Gives A Closed Interval
notes: Describe the path case constructively. Give each open interval edge a coordinate length, concatenate the coordinates along the chain, and use the smoothing repair near glued vertices so the resulting map is a smooth diffeomorphism onto a closed interval.

title: Gluing A Cycle Gives A Circle
notes: For the cycle case, stress that there is no preferred first endpoint. The same edge-length coordinate is taken modulo the total length, and the smoothing repair closes the seam so the component is smoothly modeled by a circle.

title: Disconnected Manifolds Are Componentwise
notes: Extend the connected classification without adding a new proof. Compactness gives finitely many connected components in this setting, and the argument applies to each component separately, so the whole manifold is a finite disjoint union of intervals and circles.

title: What The Appendix Buys Later
notes: Close by tying the appendix back to differential topology. The classification explains why compact one-manifolds have boundary points in pairs, because intervals contribute two endpoints and circles contribute none, a fact that powers later mod two intersection arguments.
